A_target.statement:
Let $P \subseteq \R^n$ be a [[Definition:Convex Polytope|polytope]] with $\mathbf 0$ in its [[Definition:Interior (Topology)|interior]].
Let:
:$P^\circ = \set {y: \forall x \in P: \innerprod x y \le 1}$
be its [[Definition:Polar Set|polar]].
Then the vertices of $P$ correspond to the facets of $P^\circ$, and $P^{\circ \circ} = P$.

B_source.statement:
Each point $x \ne \mathbf 0$ corresponds to the [[Definition:Half-Space|half-space]]:
:$H_x = \set {y: \innerprod x y \le 1}$
containing the origin.

substitutions.a point x of the ambient space: the half-space of all y with <x,y> at most 1
substitutions.an intersection of half-spaces: the convex hull of the corresponding points
substitutions.containment of one body in another: the reversed containment of the polars

derived.the vertices of P: the facets of the polar of P
derived.applying the correspondence twice: the polar of the polar returns P, so the correspondence is an involution

object_map.reformulation: Trade each point for the half-space it defines, converting the facet description of a body into the vertex description of its polar.

validity_conditions: The defining condition is symmetric in x and y, so the correspondence is an involution on the ambient pairing.
The origin must lie in the interior of P for the polar to be bounded; otherwise the polar is unbounded and the vertex-facet count fails.
Polarity reverses inclusion, so it exchanges descriptions as intersections of half-spaces with descriptions as convex hulls, which is exactly the exchange of facets and vertices.
proof_plan: If $x \in P \subseteq Q$ then $Q^\circ \subseteq P^\circ$, so the correspondence reverses inclusion.

As $P = \map {\operatorname {conv} } {v_1, \ldots, v_m}$, $\innerprod x y \le 1$ for all $x \in P$ {{iff}} it holds at each vertex:
:$\displaystyle P^\circ = \bigcap_{i \mathop = 1}^m H_{v_i}$
So each vertex $v_i$ gives a facet $\set {y \in P^\circ: \innerprod {v_i} y = 1}$ of $P^\circ$.

Dually, each facet $\set {x: \innerprod a x = 1}$ of $P$ gives a vertex $a$ of $P^\circ$.
By the [[Bipolar Theorem]], as $P$ is closed, convex and contains $\mathbf 0$:
:$P^{\circ \circ} = P$
{{qed}}
